stories.title: Zambian opposition leader to challenge election result in ⁠court
stories.summary: Mundubile claims his campaign documented ‘serious irregularities’ around the vote that handed President Hakainde Hichilema a second term. Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile says he will challenge the country’s presidential election result in court, alleging voting fraud in the contest that handed President Hakainde Hichilema a second term in office. “Our campaign has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results,” Mundubile said in a statement on Wednesday. While last week’s vote was largely peaceful, the opposition said intimidation and restrictions marred its campaign, concerns echoed by international election observers. The election commission declared Hichilema the winner with about 60 percent of votes in the early morning Tuesday, compared with 38 percent for Mundubile. After a relatively quiet run-up to the August 13 election in the nation of 22 million people, tensions escalated rapidly after the polls closed. The authorities arrested 11 people, including leading opposition figures in a raid that involved an exchange of gunfire while Mundubile was present. The electoral commission also suspended vote-counting for hours due to reports of violence against polling staff and ballot paper theft. UN human rights chief Volker Turk said on Wednesday he was concerned over the arrest of the opposition officials. All arrests “must be fully consistent with international human rights standards, as well as Zambian domestic law,” Turk said in a statement. Hichilema entered the race as the clear favourite after steering Zambia through a major economic turnaround and restructuring its debt. But his first term was also marked by concerns over Zambia’s political space, with opposition parties and civil society groups accusing his government of curbing dissent.

Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile says he will challenge the country’s presidential election result in court, alleging voting fraud in the contest that handed President Hakainde Hichilema a second term in office.

“Our campaign has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results,” Mundubile said in a statement on Wednesday.
While last week’s vote was largely peaceful, the opposition said intimidation and restrictions marred its campaign, concerns echoed by international election observers.
The election commission declared Hichilema the winner with about 60 percent of votes in the early morning Tuesday, compared with 38 percent for Mundubile.
After a relatively quiet run-up to the August 13 election in the nation of 22 million people, tensions escalated rapidly after the polls closed.
The authorities arrested 11 people, including leading opposition figures in a raid that involved an exchange of gunfire while Mundubile was present.
The electoral commission also suspended vote-counting for hours due to reports of violence against polling staff and ballot paper theft.
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said on Wednesday he was concerned over the arrest of the opposition officials.
All arrests “must be fully consistent with international human rights standards, as well as Zambian domestic law,” Turk said in a statement.
Hichilema entered the race as the clear favourite after steering Zambia through a major economic turnaround and restructuring its debt.
But his first term was also marked by concerns over Zambia’s political space, with opposition parties and civil society groups accusing his government of curbing dissent.
